newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO U.S. IN U.S. CENTS/LB, CIF.
Bull (95 Chemical Lean) 88 +2 on last week
Shank (90 CL) 82 +3
Trimmings (85 CL) 73 +2
Chucks (85 CL) 76 +2
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO JAPAN IN U.S. CENTS/LB CIF.
Chilled grassfed fullsets 126 +2 on last week
Chilled grassfed loin:striploin 170 -5
cube roll 225 -5
tender loin 428 n/c
Frozen Chuck/blade 90 n/c
Frozen Thick flank 104 +3
Frozen Fore/hind blended 83 n/c
Frozen Topside 104 +2
Frozen Silverside 100 +1c
Frozen Brisket 78 -1

AMLC COMMENTARY: It was a mixed week for Australian exporters. The week began with notification that Argentina will be allowed to export fresh, chilled and frozen beef to the U.S. and ended with higher export offer prices for Australian product from both Japan and U.S. A good result for Australian packers in the Korean tender meant, on the whole, it was a relatively positive week in export markets.

Under GATT, Argentina has a 20,000 tonne tariff free annual quota into the U.S. (until the current GATT agreement finishes at the end of 2000,) which they should fill this year. Above quota imports into the U.S. are levied at 29.5 percent.

It is likely that Canada will soon follow suit (as it did in the case of Uruguay) and permit Argentina entry. Although South American exporters have no country specific quota to Canada they can compete for the unallocated quota of 11,809 tonnes. In the first half of this year Canada imported 3,346 tonnes from Uruguay under these arrangements.
Once the unallocated quota has been exhausted product may also enter Canada through the supplementary import permit scheme.

Unless the U.S. and Canada grant concessions to South American exporters above and beyond their current Uruguay Round commitments, export volumes from South America into North America will be quota constrained and relatively small until the end of 2000.
Price movements in the Australian cattle markets varied this week according to quality.
Steer and heavy bullock prices were a little easier (1-2c/kg lw), medium weight steers and cow prices generally held firm, however, good trade cattle moved higher (1-2c/kg lw).

Demand from processors was a little weaker as a deterioration in margins over the past month, a function of higher cattle prices and flat beef export prices, caused a number of works to reduce production.
Slaughter in Queensland declined by 5,000 head, the first notable decline in weekly slaughter rates (aside from holiday shortened weeks) since April.
One lingering concern surrounding slaughter is the maintenance of extremely large cow kills in Queensland, which for May, were amongst the largest recorded in the last decade.
Last week, the female proportion of the cattle kill rose to 49.9 percent in Queensland.

Prices in export markets generally rose this week. U.S. imported grinding beef prices improved this week as offers of imported production declined and end-users took note of the wide differential between imported and domestic prices. Prices for imported product clawed back the majority of last week's losses, 90CL cow beef increasing 13 Ac/kg to 212 Ac/kg.

U.S. fed cattle prices slipped from 63USc/lb to 62USc/lb this week under the weight of larger production levels, easing boxed beef prices and slowing demand. Sales in the upcoming July 4 holiday weekend will be crucial in determining the direction of beef prices in the U.S. over the next month.
After this weekend, the next spike in demand in the U.S. does not occur until buying begins for the Labor Day holiday on September 1.

In Japan, wholesale markets showed signs of improvement for the first time in many months. In the Chubu and Kansai regions, most cuts were reported to have traded well. This strength in wholesale markets flowed through to export offer prices. Prices of most imported items increased (the exception was individual loin cuts), grassfed fullsets rose 5Ac/kg to 329Ac/kg.
Increases in frozen product prices were assisted by a recovery in the U.S. manufacturing beef market.
These improvements may also represent some increased trading in lieu of the "Obon" Holiday period in mid August.
Australian exporters fared well in the latest Korean tender, securing 90 percent of the grassfed portion.
This represented 684 tonnes of grassfed fullsets and 3590 tonnes of grassfed quarters which has to be shipped to Korea by early August.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
